Mr. Speaker, perhaps I have undertaken a task that is beyond my ability because I am going to venture into the professional realm this afternoon. I am not professionally minded by any means, nor have I had any training whatsoever along that line. I pride
The Address-Mr. Leader

myself on being a practical man though, and I believe even in the professions-and the medical profession especially-one can be practical.
The speech from the throne declares that provision should be made to expand research activities, and that will be the basis of my remarks this afternoon. I am going to speak on only one phase of it, and that is the phase of cancer research. Coupled with that I wish to give the story of Doctor J. R. Davidson, 232 Somerset block, Winnipeg, and some of the results of his investigations of over thirty years in searching for a cure, or as he puts it, a preventive and a possible cure for cancer.
This matter was introduced in this chamber last year by two hon. members. It is true I suggested that these hon. members might mention the case of Doctor J. R. Davidson, because they had both known him well, and at least one hon. gentleman had been associated with him for thirty or thirty-five years. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) was the first to bring the matter before the house. He was kind enough to mention my name and to say that I certainly appeared to be improved in health as compared with previous years. Following that mention of my name I received literally hundreds of letters from all over Canada. I did not know that the newspapers had got hold of it, but evidently some of the newspapers in the east did, because I received some of the most pathetic letters I have ever read. One woman wrote to ask me what she would have to do in order to bring her husband, who was afflicted with cancer, to Winnipeg to undergo the treatment prescribed by Doctor Davidson. I asked Doctor Davidson if I should tell her to bring her husband to Winnipeg for treatment, but he replied, "Harry, don't; I have far more than I can attend to now." Two months later I received a letter in which this lady told me that her husband had passed on.
I mention that instance to indicate the ravages of this, the world's greatest scourge. The other hon. member who mentioned this subject was the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden). He is a medical man, and I was particularly anxious that he, with his knowledge of the situation, should bring up this matter in parliament. It was not that I wanted to shirk my responsibility, but I told him that in a few days I was going home to continue my treatments with Doctor Davidson, and that in my opinion he could deal with the matter much better than any hon. member, because he had the advantage of having known Doctor Davidson for so long.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And he is sincere.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is no question about that; he is one hundred per cent sincere.
I do not intend to tell the story of Doctor Davidson's work or to outline his treatment, though we have discussed it many times. I am a patient of his, and from my place in this house I say that he has done me a lot of good. I am not going to say that he has cured me, because I have had cancer for twelve years. I am sure he would be the last man in the world to say he could cure me; but he did say, "I think I can help you," and that is just what he has done. I should like, however, to recall the gist of what was said by the hon. member for St. Boniface, who, as I have said, has been associated with Doctor Davidson for thirty-five years. He pointed out that medical associations, even as far away as Rochester, have been kept informed of Doctor Davidson's work, and he told us that Doctor Davidson has carried on his work on his own premises and at his own expense. Finally he paid tribute to Doctor Davidson as a doctor and as a good citizen.
Hon. members who are interested, as I am sure all hon. members are, may find the story of Doctor Davidson's professional investigations in Hansard for Wednesday, July 14, 1943, in the speeches of the two hon. members I have mentioned. I should like, however, to quote from the discussion that took place at that time, in order to show the interest that was taken in what these hon. members had to say. The hon. member for Fort William asked, as reported at page 4800 of Hansard for last session:
Will anything be done in regard to this matter? I do not wish to press the minister too hard, but the people who have been cured are most anxious that all the scientific research which has been carried on by Doctor Davidson shall not be lost.
The minister, who has been entirely sympathetic to every effort to have the work of Doctor Davidson investigated, replied:
There is 'a committee functioning now in conjunction with the national research council which investigates cases of this kind, and I am sure it is important that this be done in connection with this matter. Certainly I shall bring this discussion to the attention of that committee.
If the records are consulted it will be found that within a very few days the minister did bring the matter to the attention of this committee, which is a branch of the research council. Then the leader of the Progressive Conservative party (Mr. Graydon) had a word1 to say which showed his kindly interest:
Has this work by Doctor Davidson been under consideration by the national research council?

The Address-Mr. Leader
To this question the minister replied: "Not to my knowledge." Then the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall), continuing the debate, said:
I think we were all very glad to hear the statement made by the hon. member for St. Boniface; the members of the medical profession can make valuable contributions to the debates of this house.
This leads me to remark that we can all make valuable contributions to the debates of this house, but it will take more than debate to settle many of the difficulties which confront Canada, and particularly the matter with which I am dealing to-day.
Dyson Carter, a scientist, had an article in Saturday Night of October 23 in which he quotes the authoritative Journal of the American Medical Association as saying editorially:
The only hope of solving fundamental problems of cancer lies in research.
Then in the draft national health bill the first explanatory note reads:
To place within the grasp of the people of Canada the benefits of a comprehensive scheme of health insurance, designed and organized for * the prevention and cure of disease and the conservation of health.
In the proposed bill the statement is made that deaths from cancer number 12,000 annually, but I believe that in 1942 that number had increased to 14,000, and since cancer is on the increase it is only reasonable to suppose that in this year upon which we have just entered the number will be even greater, perhaps 16.000. Dyson Carter concludes his article, which is based on Doctor Davidson's work and the speeches made in this house last session, by saying:
One savage fact to strike home the truth: so rapidly is cancer increasing that to-day, on our continent, twenty-four veterans of the great war are entering hospital with this disease every twenty-four hours.
As a rule, Mr. Speaker, it is not nice to deal with one's personal affairs in a public way. Sometimes the less said about one's own personal affairs, the better it is for everybody, but it is necessary for my purpose to bring my own particular case to the attention of the house. I told you a few moments ago that I have suffered from cancer for many years. Of course I did not know this at the start. I finally went to Rochester and my trouble was diagnosed as cancer. This was arrived at not by a physical examination but by the exploration of my abdomen. They told me-I shall deal more fully with this in a few moments-that nothing could be done for me, but if I would be good I might live a long while. Then comes a joke which perhaps should never be told in parliament.
However, it is so good that I want to tell it to-day. They told me not to do any hard work or to have any mental worry and I immediately said, "Will I be able to attend to mv duties at Ottawa?" and a doctor said, "Oh, yes."
I was persuaded to go and see Doctor Davidson. I found him a very modest man, reluctant to speak of his achievements. He would not claim that he could cure cancer, but he was enthusiastic in his belief that cancer could be prevented by the proper diet. He said that all of his experiments led to that conclusion. May I repeat in this house that Doctor Davidson has helped me. If I am allowed I should like to tell you how simple and easy it has been to effect a better condition of life. For ten years I had been constipated and in constant danger of bowel stoppage. He said, "The first thing we must do for you, Mr. Leader, is to get nature functioning properly; we will prescribe a certain diet for you and see if we can get you back to normal." I followed that diet religiously. It consisted of vitamin pills, wheat germ on my porridge and radio-malt twice a day. I am able to eat anything that agrees with me. I have followed this diet religiously and for nearly a year after starting Doctor Davidson's treatment I have not had a laxative. He has helped me to regain my health. As Doctor Davidson says, it is all so simple that most people will not believe ' it. However, many people are now following his advice.
I started this dietary treatment and then commenced with his cure. It must be remembered that he did not say he could cure me; he never told me he could cure cancer, but he feels he is on the right track and I believe that he is. He has a preparation which he has developed-I will call it a serum but that may not be the proper term-which the hon. member for St. Boniface referred to last year. I could go into this at greater detail to-day but I have not the time. I started to take his treatments and they have done me a lot of good.
I was taking these three times a week, and one day when I was in Winnipeg I went to the office of Doctor J. R. Davidson and his secretary told me that he was sick in the hospital with a heart attack.
I had1 feared that something like this would happen, because he had been working entirely too hard with the very limited staff which he had at that time. I asked at which hospital and then I went out to see him and found he was feeling a little better. But he had suffered a heart attack even though he was able to come back to his office in a few
The Address-Mr. Leader

days. Then I realized that it was time for me to move. At that time it was perhaps three or four months since the matter had been, mentioned in the House of Commons and still no action had been taken. I wanted to keep in the background until I was able to rise in my place before you and offer myself as a living example of this man's work. I wanted to be sure; I did not want to try to put anything over. However, I thought it was time for me to get busy. I called up my friend, the hon. member for St. Boniface, and asked him whom I should approach in the medical profession in Winnipeg in order to direct attention to the condition of Doctor J. R. Davidson. He told me to call up Doctor Cadham, the pathologist in the Manitoba medical college. I talked to him over the telephone. He said he knew Doctor Davidson and had great respect for him. I asked if he knew he was in the hospital and he said that he did not, that he was sorry to hear that. I told him that there was a danger of this man passing, and that with his passing would perish the secret of his years of investigation. He then told me that I would find Doctor Davidson a very difficult man to deal with, that he had worked with him during the first years of his experiments but that he always played a lone game, that he would not play ball with the rest of the profession. He told me that they had investigated his early work but that there , was nothing there. I told him that I had been to Rochester; I explained my experience there, and I offered to go to Doctor Cadham that afternoon to have a physical examination. I received no encouragement. I told him that if the medical association of Winnipeg would appoint a committee I would come down any day since I was in Winnipeg three times a week. I did not receive any invitation. When I suggested that the research council should take this up he did say that that was the proper body to deal with the matter.
Right here I might just as well say that the research council has a representative in Winnipeg. You may wonder why I mention names, but I do so because I believe in telling the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Doctor Thorlakson is the representative in Winnipeg of the research council, and I have been told that he is absolutely opposed to any investigation being made into the work of Doctor J. R. Davidson. He represents a body that is going to investigate, or should at the present time be investigating the work of Doctor Davidson. I then wrote to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), and I should like to read

this letter because it outlines in a concise manner the situation as it existed at that time. The letter reads:
Dear Mr. Mackenzie:
I am again drawing to your attention the case of Doctor J. R, Davidson of Winnipeg, Manitoba. You will remember the reference to the doctor's work when the matter was mentioned in the house last session by Daniel Mclvor, M.P., and Doctor Howden, M.P. I also mentioned the matter to you during the recent national Liberal convention in Ottawa.
Apparently nothing is being done to check officially, the work of Doctor Davidson in his search for prevention and a possible cure for cancer notwithstanding the publicity given in several magazines and first-class newspapers.
As a patient of Doctor Davidson and as a public man, I can assure you that I am deeply interested in Doctor Davidson's cancer experiments, and believe that he has long passed the experimental stage and that his work should be given the proper official recognition. Therefore I would respectfully ask you. the responsible minister in such cases, what procedure I should follow that would hasten an official investigation.
Within the last month Doctor Davidson was sent to the hospital with a heart attack. He is again attending his patients, but the danger of collapse is ever present. Can we afford to sit idly by and see this Canadian doctor's work in cancer research perish with his passing?
Will you please designate the procedure that I should follow in getting some immediate definite action in this supremely important matter.
The minister answered promptly. I am not going to quote his letter. In fact, I wrote him again soon after that, and again the minister answered promptly. But I wish to quote a paragraph from his letter just to confirm the argument which I made a moment ago in regard to the attitude of some of the medical men at. Winnipeg and some of those who are higher up. This paragraph says:
Two items of information have come to the department recently by way of gossip:-(1) that the medical men in Winnipeg, many of whom were quite outspoken in regard to the hopefulness of something genuinely good coming out of Doctor Davidson's studies, have in recent months apparently been less hopeful. The second point is that we have been informed, that the Doctor, who is 73 years of age, has suffered a stroke or some other serious disability.
I perhaps was responsible for the latter rumour.

No, not that it is very serious at all, but it just makes me a little dubious of the outcome of the investigation which is now taking place in Winnipeg.
I learned in correspondence with the minister that the research council had never received any request from Doctor J. R. Davidson for any aid in his experiments. When I heard that. I got busy and advised Doctor Davidson that that was what he would have to do. The research council went on to say that they were prepared to deal with the matter in a judicial manner after a request had been received. I told Doctor Davidson that he would have to have his findings put in concrete form, substantiated and certified by medical men who had dealt with his particular cases. He told me that he had done that just the night before. "I sent it away last night," he said. Then I found out that others were working besides myself, many others, in fact, but the man I speak of in particular lives in Regina, and he says that his wife was cured by Doctor Davidson. This man had found out that an application for aid was necessary; I think he supplied the information to Doctor Davidson, and the request for aid from the research council was sent down, I believe, on December 14. Acknowledgment was made on January 5. A questionnaire was sent at that time to Doctor Davidson by Doctor Ettinger, of Kingston, secretary of the research council, I understand, asking the doctor to fill out the questionnaire so that the council would have a basis on which to make an investigation. That questionnaire was sent back January 25. I have here the questionnaire, filled out by Doctor Davidson himself, which I shall not read.

speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me, I called to see Doctor Davidson twice with reference to someone I knew, and he showed me a long list of people whom his serum or treatment had evidently cured. Has the hon. member seen that list?

speechtext:
Yes, and I have also with me the addresses of some of the patients. I will give them a little later. I have them here.
I want to give the house a little personal experience that I had with Doctor Davidson and his work. Doctor Davidson emphasizes the prevention of cancer rather than its cure. His original theory that a nutritional deficiency in diet causes cancer has been ibundantly proved by his experiments with mice, and the serum treatment he has developed is a direct result of his research work in discovering the cause of cancer. He has told me many times that his
deep concern centred in finding preventive measures to control the incidence of cancer rather than in finding a cure, where a cure so often is impossible. The old adage that an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure applies with terriffic force in matters of public health.
May I now give some concrete examples of Doctor Davidson's work. I have before me cases certified by medical practitioners and by representatives of clinics which have made investigations of cases treated by Doctor Davidson where the cancer had cleared up and the people were now evidently in good health and showed no symptoms of cancer. Let me refer to my own condition.
Here is the report from Doctor Waugh of the Mayo clinic, Rochester. I asked Doctor Waugh if I had his permission to use this letter and I told him about Doctor Davidson in Winnipeg. Doctor Waugh sent a copy of this letter to Doctor Davidson and he closes by saying that if he could render help he would be glad to do so. The doctor found a condition in my abdomen which had been there for many years and which had become so extensive that it was not even wise to try to find the primary site. He said my case was hopeless.	.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Your case?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes; he said my case was hopeless. He went on to say that he had thought of doing some short-circuiting because of potential bowel obstruction, of which so many people die, but he said even that was impossible. Doctor Waugh told me when I left Rochester that he has known of cases like my own, carcinoid tumour, where people have lived for twelve or fifteen years after the condition was surveyed. If you will recall, sir, what I told you about this vitamin diet which the doctor prescribed for me, and remember what he did to take care of that potential obstruction, you will realize what Dr. Davidson has done for me and is doing for hundreds of people in Manitoba at the present time. It is no exaggeration to say that Dr. Davidson's fame is becoming known all over the world. He is getting letters from Australia. The other day I read a letter in his office inviting him to California, telling him that there are a number of institutions in that state which would be glad to have him continue his experience in those institutions. I said "Doctor, you would not want to leave Canada?"- remember he is seventy-four years old-and he replied, "No; this is my home, I want to stay here." But this goes to show that unless some effective action is taken immediately, either this man will leave Canada and go to
The Address-Mr. Leader

another country, or, on account of his age, pass on and we shall lose the value of his experiments.
I should like to say something about the case of Mrs. J. N. de Stein, of Regina. An abdominal operation on November 22, 1941, was performed by Doctor J. A. Brown. At that time an extensive cancer condition was found. The pathological report confirmed the diagnosis as cancer. The patient also received radiation treatment, but no hope was held for her recovery. Since November, 1942, the patient has been under the care of Doctor J. R. Davidson. On examination by Doctor John H. Gunn on December 15, 1942, she was found to be in excellent health. Mr. de Stein is using all the persuasive powers at his command to see if something cannot be done in the way of investigation. A statement was published in the papers in which he said that owing to Doctor Davidson his wife was completely cured of cancer and has been living at her home, happy, and in good health. This is the tj'pe of record with which the research council will have to deal.
I come now to the case of Irwin Cowan, 202 Brooklyn street, Winnipeg. I give addresses in case some hon. members may wish to write to these people and get'their own personal story. This boy was admitted to St. Boniface hospital on July 24, 1936, under the care of Doctor Edwin Corrigan. He had a mass of glands removed from the neck, but no pathological report was made at that time. He returned to hospital, in January, 1937, and had more glands removed. A pathological report determined the case as cancer. The patient returned again in December, 1938, and another gland was removed. Since that time he has been under the care of Doctor J. R. Davidson. An X-ray examination on December 2, 1943, conducted by Dr. Wheeler, revealed the boy as absolutely free from cancer. This boy was a patient of Doctor Davidson and is still under his supervision.
Here is another case, that of S. S. Coulter, 212 Maryland street, Winnipeg. This man was referred to the Abbott clinic on October 26, 1939, by Doctor J. R. Davidson. In 1937 the man had an operation for cancer of the lower lip. Another operation was performed in October, 1939, and a third operation on May 22, 1940, when more portions of the cancer were removed. On May 29 the patient was sent home. On December 3, 1943, he returned for examination. There is no evidence of any recurrence either in the lips or in the glands of the neck. The patient is enjoying the best of health and is apparently free from

cancer. He has been under Doctor Davidson's care for some years and is still under his supervision.
Here is the case of Mrs. A. MacDougall, of Pembina, North Dakota. She had a tumour removed in 1933. It returned in 1938, and she was again operated on, on October 23, 1939. The pathological report pronounced cancer of the breast. This patient has been undergoing treatment by Doctor Davidson, and an examination by Doctor Wheeler found her free from cancer and in excellent health. I met this woman in Doctor Davidson's office one day, and she told me that she was in perfect health, but that when she came to Winnipeg she always wanted to look up the doctor who had made her well.
Another case is that of Mrs. J. Catton, of 1308 Portage avenue, Winnipeg. She was sent to hospital for operation re cancer in brea,st. The pathological report was "cancer," and the cancer was removed! in July, 1942. Examination in November showed no sign of recurrence and the patient appeared in good health. This is a report by Doctor Neil H. Blakie.

speechtext:
I am sure that all hon. members were glad to hear the opening remarks in the speech from the throne, that war conditions had improved. I was glad to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leaders of other groups, and also the member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair), when he spoke to-day, warn the house that while the situation has improved, the war is not ended. Indeed, far from its being won, there is much fighting and much suffering and there will be many casualties before peace comes.
Like other members of this group who have already spoken in this debate, I welcome the modest programme of social betterment mentioned' in the speech. I wish it were as comprehensive and as important as friends to my right fear it is. Possibly they are thinking of it in terms of vote-catching while I am thinking of it in terms of social improvement, which makes all the difference in the world. Some objections have been made in various places to this modest programme of social reform, to the effect that it would detract from the country's war effort. Personally I do not agree with that. In my opinion, not only will it not detract from our war effort but it will do much to improve it.
Defeating Hitler is not the only objective in this war. While that is very important we must also have as an objective the elimination of those conditions that create Hitlers. If we 109-15
do not remove the cause, other Hitlers will arise. I do not believe that there can be a better time than the present, when the minds of our people are attuned to change, for making social improvements that are long overdue.
I was astonished that there was nothing in the speech from the throne in regard to labour. If it were not realized before, I think it is realized now that industrial relations in this war constitute one of the spots in our whole war effort where we have fallen down. In previous sessions, since the war began I have done my humble best to try to get this government to realize the direction in which we have been moving. No heed was taken of the dangers I was trying to point out. The result is that never has discontent been so rampant as it is at the present time.
Just before coming to Ottawa, along with other members of parliament from the greater Vancouver district, I attended a meeting of the Vancouver, New Westminster and district trades and labour council, affiliated to the American Federation of Labor. In the language of the street, we heard an earful from the three hundred delegates present who represented some 22,000 workers. Since that time I have received resolutions from labour organizations all across Canada denouncing the government's latest wage control order. To put on record what I believe to be the universal attitude of organized labour, I cannot do better than read a resolution passed by the Trades and Labour Council of my own city:
Whereas the new wage control order, P.C. 9384, announced by the government on December 10 following a broadcast on the subject by the Prime Minister, reflects the further intensification of an anti-labour attitude in official government circles that has long stood in the way of implementation of a constructive labour policy in Canada;
And, whereas we are alarmed at the increasing influence over government of big financial interests and large industrialists so clearly demonstrated by many of the orders in council adversely affecting the workers of Canada;
And. whereas said wage control order is in opposition to all the basic principles of the trade union movement and against the recognized principles of freedom and justice;
And, whereas there is a growing tendency of ruling the country by order in council instead of by acts of parliament:
Therefore be it resolved that we urge upon our elected representatives in the dominion parliament the immediate need of them performing the duties for which they were elected and to insist on the reestablishment of the rights of parliament.
Be it further resolved that we most emphatically protest the refusal of the government to heed the expressed wish of labour for a more constructive policy.
And be it further resolved that we hereby demand the immediate withdrawal of the new wartime wage control order, 1943. P.C. 9384, and we hereby authorize President Bengough to

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

make any representations on our behalf, and promise to support him in any action he may recommend us to follow.
That, I believe, is a fair expression of the feeling of organized labour throughout Canada, and I think members of parliament who sit here year in and year out and see these things being done without a word of protest have something to account for to the labour people in the constituencies which those members represent. I believe that members of parliament are beginning to realize this.
I have in my hand this morning's Globe and Mail in which is reported a meeting held yesterday at Hamilton. I am not going to read all that is here reported. I will give two paragraphs that indicate that organized labour is at last receiving some support from their representatives. This report states:
A surprise feature of the rally was the admission by two local Liberal M.P.'s . . .
I will not give their names.
. . . that the members of parliament have not been consulted on such matters.

speechtext: The paper does give their names.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton East and the hon. member for Wentworth.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
. . . that the members of parliament have not been consulted on such matters.
It goes on to quote what these men said, and it is as follows:
The government is run by a bureaucracy ; the members are nothing, and I fr.ankly admit it. If the order had gone through the house it would have been better prepared.
Then the other hon. member spoke along somewhat similar lines. He had a good word to say for the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell). If it. was not a good word it was at least not a bad word. He said:
The Minister of Labour is not as bad as you think he is, but his hands are tied by these men who supposedly guide the destinies of this country.
I have tried to help the Minister of Labour. I am afraid, however, that he thought when I was trying to help him that I was really criticizing him. I wish to say that I was not. I tried to help him privately by advice, but it appears that my advice was not taken. I am not as much surprised as are those members of parliament, or as the representatives of labour at this new order. It is a legitimate successor to all the wage control orders that preceded it, P.C. 7440 of December, 1940, 8253 of October, 1941, and 5963 of July, 1942.

Each of these orders took a little bit away from labour and the government got away with it. The government seeing that labour stood for it took a little bit more next time. I have not the time, and it is really not necessary to analyse this new order in detail. Its various' points have been touched on by other hon. membfc, by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) and by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) as well as by other members.
This group has been advocating adequate labour representation on war boards. When the national war labour board was first organized under P.C. 8253, it had nine members-a chairman, four members representing employers and four members representing employees. A year ago that was changed and we had a board made up of three-a chairman, one member representing employers and one member representing the workers. Under the new order the board is composed of six members-a chairman, a vice-chairman, two members representing the public, one member representing the employers and one member representing the workers. Organized labour believes, and I agree, that under this new set-up they have one representative out of six. It may be said that the chairman, the vice-chairman, and the two members representing the public may be taken as representing labour as well as the employers, but from my experience I would say that any person the present government appoints to a board of this kind, if he is not appointed with the approval of organized labour, will have the employer's point of view. I submit that is not the way to give labour equal representation on war boards.
The order is bad in many ways. The machinery for appeals is inadequate. Regional boards have really no power at all in the present set-up. They are merely agents or the puppets of the national war labour board. The regional boards -must submit every decision and every finding made to the national board; the national war labour board of itself, without these findings being submitted to it at all, is authorized to review and vary ih any way it sees fit the findings of a regional board, and the decisions of the national board become the decision in that particular case.
The hon. member for Vancouver North pointed out for the first time in this house the worst section of this order, namely section 14, which outlines the purposes of the order. I shall read it:
14. It is the purpose of this order
(a) to provide for the establishment of wage rates incorporating therein cost of living bonuses, payable in respect of the rise in the cost of living.

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis
I submit that is not correct. The order does not provide for the establishment of wage rates. They have frozen the present wage rates and incorporated in those wage rates the cost of living bonus. Therefore the first paragraph gives an altogether wrong impression of the purposes of the board.
(b)	to stabilize the wage structure in Canada established in this manner in order to maintain stability in prices and prevent increases in the general cost of living; and
(c)	to provide machinery for an orderly rectification of any gross inequalities and injustices in wage rates so established, in so far as this is possible consistently with the paramount principle of the maintenance of stability in prices, and this_ order shall be administered and enforced to give effect to these purposes.
As was pointed out this afternoon, it can be clearly seen that the national war labour board or the regional boards have authority only to deal with cases where gross inequalities and injustices are apparent, but if in the opinion of the board the removal of those gross inequalities and injustices should interfere with the maintenance of the price structure they are to leave them there, they are to freeze inequalities and injustices. It is no wonder that organized labour resents a policy of that kind.
I should like to make this quite clear. As I have said in this house on many occasions, I am not opposed to wage control and price stabilization. I am convinced they are absolutely essential at the present time. I will go farther than that and say that this government is to be commended for its achievements in that regard; but I submit it is not fair and it is not just to put the burden of price stabilization on the shoulders of those least able to bear it-the underpaid workers. That is what this order in council does.
I should like to read a short paragraph from the majority report of the national war labour board in regard to the matter to which I have just referred. The report states that a wage of fifty cents an hour, $24 a week, could not provide a decent or a healthy standard of living for the heads of families. I agree. But this order in council freezes wages not at fifty cents an hour but at thirty-five cents an hour. I should like to point out that it has long been an axiom of the capitalists that in the carrying on of their business they should not have to draw on capital assets. This applies equally to workers. The capital of the worker is his health and energy; and if he is compelled to live, as he will be compelled to live under this order in council, on a wage rate which does not give him a standard of living sufficient to maintain his health and strength, then he is using up the only assets he has.
100-15J
This is the view of the national war labour board, and I suggest to hon. members that they read the majority and minority reports of that board, for they make good reading.
I derived a great deal of comfort from reading the majority report, because it bears out almost every contention in regard to labour that I have raised in this house since 1940. At page 17 the report says:
Even in a war economy a policy which consigns human beings to economic serfdom when a large portion of the community escapes it is incompatible with the ideal6 on behalf of which we are waging war.
I agree with the national war labour board, and I believe the government must agree also. If they do agree, then they will have to dp something about it; at least they will have to leave persons working for a wage of less than fifty cents an hour free to negotiate for increases in wages without being tied down by the condition mentioned in this order, of maintaining prices.
I would and could and do take exception to various other sections of the order in council under review. There is the provision forbidding strikes and providing penalties for striking. Personally I do not believe in the strike-as a weapon. Sometimes, however, the workers have no other recourse, but I believe that it is a rather unintelligent weapon and that it should be used only under the greatest provocation. But a time comes when workers' reach the stage where it makes no difference to them whether they remain at work or go on strike. When that time comes they will strike, I do not care how many laws are on the statute books saying they shall not; and there is nothing you can do about it. It would be just as effective to pass a law saying mules must not balk as to pass a law against strikes, because when the burden becomes intolerable both men and mules will balk.
The order is totalitarian in its conception and, as I pointed out in regard to strikes, it is foolish and cannot be enforced. The sections that place the onus of proof in connection with violations of the order upon employers or employees in my opinion is wrong; I believe it is something new in British jurisprudence, and we should not tolerate it at this time. I believe we should more and more compare our actions with the ideals for which, we are fighting; find if we do so we shall find that this practice of placing the onus of proof upon the accused and many of our other practices are altogether out of harmony with our contention that in this war we are fighting for freedom. There is also the provision in the order which gives the national board the right to change agreements, to reduce wages, to change hourly rates to piece work rates,
22S
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

and so on. This takes away the whole function of organized labour to negotiate wage agreements.
In concluding what I have to say on this matter, I suggest to the government that as an indication of its good intentions toward labour it refrain from putting this order into effect [DOT]on the date mentioned, which I believe is February 15. Further I would suggest to the government and in particular to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) that the whole question of the stabilization of wages and industrial relations be referred to the standing committee on industrial and international relations. Let that committee, composed of members of this house, hear what representatives of labour and of employers have to say. There is no reason why that could not be done. Officials of the government could appear before the committee, if they wished, and in the presence of representatives of labour outline the difficulties they have to meet. I am sure that if we had a full discussion of these questions some satisfactory means of dealing with them would be found. I also associate myself with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) and with the leader of this group that this committee should be divided, that there is sufficient material under those two headings for two committees. I see no reason why a person who is conversant with labour matters would of necessity be conversant with international .affairs or vice versa.

Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock I was referring to the government's labour policies and their inadequacy in the situation in which we now find ourselves. When one looks back on our labour policy and our labour difficulties since the war began; when one realizes the resistance of employers to collective bargaining, the failure of the government to give labour representation on war boards, the resistance, I believe, of both employers and the government to the inauguration of labour-management production boards, one really feels that we are not progressing very fast. I should like to quote once more from the report of the national war labour board inquiry. I quote from the majority award because it is signed by the chairman and the representative of the employers, although I believe the minority report is just as worthy of consideration. The majority report has this to say:
(Mr. Maclnnis.]
To any one with an eye to see and an ear to hear, it must be clear that labour, more particularly organized labour, is suffering from a sense of frustration as far as the war effort is concerned. It wants to take a responsible part in production, the planning of production and the revising of planning when the same becomes necessary.
We expect the cooperation of labour and we do nothing to give labour an opportunity to show that it can cooperate. The failure of the government's labour policy, the failure of the government to understand labour's place in modern production and indeed the government's hostility to organized labour are aptly demonstrated by two orders in council. One of these, recognizing collective bargaining in crown companies, was passed in 1942, in the third year of the war. The other was tabled a few days ago by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Martin). This order in council sets up an industrial production cooperation board. In the fifth year of the war we have come to the stage where we recognize, at least on paper, the value of labour's cooperation in industry.
I should like to say something about the proposal in the speech from the throne to pay family allowances. There is not much I can say because I do not know exactly what is implied in the reference in the speech. It is extremely vague and we cannot offer an opinion in regard to the particular legislation until we know what it is going to be. But I should like to know if this is part of the government's social security legislation, or is it proposed as a substitute for low wages? From -the way it has come up it appears to me that it is a substitute for low wages. In the majority report of the national war labour board two alternatives are set out. Labour must be permitted to bargain up to a certain wage or provision must be made for paying family allowances. If it is the purpose of these family allowances to supplement low wages I am opposed to family allowances.

I am glad to hear that.
That being the case, there is no reason why I should say anything more on the subject at this time. Real family allowances will be supported by the group with which I am associated.
I should like to make a brief reference to a matter which was referred to on Thursday last by several speakers. I refer to the question of refugees and immigration. In the few minutes I have at my disposal I should like to make some comments on the statements made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) when he spoke. I am glad to see he is just taking his seat.

The use of the word "precipice" in this connection is very revealing because it indicates a fear of reforms by my hon. friend and his party. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Tremblay) and the seconder (Mr. Tucker) of the address. These two members made a notable contribution in the first war and are to-day serving again.
I should also like to offer to the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) my most sincere congratulations - upon the very fine .address that he made to the house this afternoon. He gave to the members an insight of what our fighting boys overseas are thinking about and the kind of Canada they wish to come back to. This young -member is typical of the young Canada of to-day who rare serving in the army, the navy, or the air force and writing the name of Canada high up on the scroll of history. This young member is attached to the air force,, and I think all hon. members will agree that Canada is especially proud of the boys who serve in the air force. Only a short time ago these were the boys who filled our schools and playing fields. Yet to-day they are flying with silver wings [DOT] to blast the enemy wherever he may be found, and in their flights they bring hope and comfort to millions of people, now slaves, that the day of victory and peace is coming nearer. It is to that type of young man who represents young Canada to-day that we who stay at home owe so much, and our first duty must be to see that these young men will be fully reestablished and rehabilitated in the peacetime life of this country.
As was well pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver North this afternoon several times during his speech, our boys who are fighting to-day do not want charity; they do not expect charity. All they want is the opportunity to have a stake in Canada, the ;hance to reestablish themselves in the peacetime economy of this great country. It is quite fitting, therefore, that the speech from the throne should indicate that there is to be a full-time minister charged with the administration of soldiers' affairs.
Another very interesting announcement in the speech from the throne was that at last some further attention is to be paid to mustering-out pay for the men in the armed forces. There have been many debates in this house on the welfare of soldiers returning to civilian life, and members of all parties have indicated their earnest desire that the very best that Canada can do for these young men should be done. Many of the measures

passed by this house and many of the measures described in the press indicate in glowing terms the things we are proposing to do, but unfortunately when we see how some of these things work out, we find they are not so satisfactory. An indication of this was given only a week ago to-morrow when the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) tabled in the house two new orders in council whereby the grave injustice in the matter of pay to soldiers in hospital has been corrected. I for one find it very difficult, to understand why such a condition was allowed to exist until the first day of February, 1944. The minister must have full knowledge of the many sore spots of which the returned boys complain. But it seems as though the government will never act until they are forced to do so by public opinion through the press. One illustration of that is what happened in regard to Christie street hospital. Hon. members will remember the debate which took place in this house last year. It was not until after that debate and the clamour that arose in the press that any change was made in the most unsatisfactory and disgraceful conditions which existed at that hospital. Canada expects that we shall provide well for our returned soldiers, and I am quite sure that the minister found out through the clamour which arose that the general public was not satisfied with the treatment our boys were receiving at Christie street hospital.
I have learned from my experience in talking to discharged soldiers-and there are many from my section of Ontario who have been in action overseas and who have now returned home-that there are many things of which they complain. As I mentioned before, these men do not want charity; they do not expect any benefit that is handed out in a grudging spirit by the pensions department or any other department of government. These men have a first claim upon the country, and they are legally entitled to full compensation for any injury to their-health through either sickness or war wounds. What must any soldier who has served overseas and gone through experiences there far worse than any described in Dante's "Inferno" think when he comes before the pension board and is brushed aside by some hard-hearted official or when he is confronted with a form letter with his name typed on the top and that newly-coined phrase that is now being used on the form letters "pre-enlistment-not aggravated by military service," or when he is told that he has no apparent disability? Our soldiers are entitled to the most sympathetic consideration by the officials of the pensions department. It was

The Address-Mr. White
not lor the kind of treatment that I have described that these young men gave up everything and went overseas to defend freedom. In many cases the long and unreasonable delay in dealing with pension cases is most embarrassing to the soldier. It is quite true that he receives certain benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act, but in many cases these benefits are exhausted before his pension claim is adjusted. It is many, many years since the scale of pensions has been revised in any 'way. Various other benefits, such as pay, clothing, and dependents' allowance, have been increased. Labour has a cost of living bonus; it is enjoying much higher wages than it received before the war. But in the matter of pensions payable to soldiers there have been no changes for years, and I think it is only reasonable and fair to expect that a soldier drawing a full disability pension should have some reasonable increase to cover the increased cost of living.
Many hon. members have spoken about the clothing allowance. I was very glad to hear the announcement of the minister that it had been increased to $65; but, along with other members, I wish to say that in my opinion that is not sufficient. I for one would be much interested in having one of the defence ministers place on Hansard a table showing how the sum of $65 is broken up to enable a soldier to refit himself for civilian life. A soldier while he is in the army is very proud of the uniform he wears. I think the very least we can do is fit him up properly so that when he steps out into civilian life he will still be proud of his appearance, and I do not think he can do so on a grant of $65.
Then there is the question of the amount of pensions payable to officers and men. I have always felt that a soldier, whether an officer or a private, if he should lose an eye or a limb, should receive the same amount of pension. Rank should not affect the award in any way, because both officer and private have to compete in civilian life.
I should like to draw to the attention of the minister of pensions the case of soldiers who have a pensionable disability of less than fifty per cent. On the death of the soldier with a disability of less than fifty per cent his widow does not continue to receive a pension; yet it has always seemed to me that during the lifetime of the husband the pension department recognized the right of the wife. It seems to me that after the death of the husband the wife is more than ever in need of that help.
The hon. member for Vancouver North dealt this afternoon with the matter of the very small rehabilitation grant, which at the nresent
time is only one month's pay and allowances. I was very glad to see the statement in the speech from the throne that this matter is to be investigated, and I sincerely hope that the amount granted will not be small, but liberal, and that when the amount is decided upon the provisions will be made retroactive to cover all soldiers discharged to date.
Each session many hon. members speak of the insurance principle, and I think the min-.ster of pensions will agree that this provision should be reinserted in the Pension Act. I for one have never heard in this house any explanations of why this provision was taken out. Surely a man who served in the army in Canada is entitled, whether on duty or on leave, to the benefit of the Pension Act. It is quite true that under certain amendments-I believe it is section II-there are compassionate provisions, but I do not think that is enough. They are of a charitable nature, and at the best they are only temporary. There have been many cases where soldiers discharged in "E" category received no pension. To date the number of men discharged from the armed forces exceeds 100,000, yet the number receiving pensions is somewhat between five and six thousand. This seems rather hard to justify, where a man enlists and is placed iq "A" category. Hon. members who know anything about the method of the medical examination of a soldier will agree that it is a thorough, rigid and complete examination, including X-ray. If that man is accepted for service and placed in "A" category, and after service in Canada or overseas is discharged in "E" category, it is only reasonable that any disability should be attributed to war service. This is not now the case. Every hon. member must know of many cases where soldiers have been discharged in "E" category and have received no pension. How can any medical doctor, examining a soldier upon his discharge, say, two or three years after his enlistment, that his present disability is not due to war service, when on the medical history sheet there is no record of a disability? Unfortunately, however, the onus is always on the soldier to prove his case. Surely in any case where there is doubt the soldier should receive the benefit of that doubt, and private soldiers should not have continually to fight the pensions department to get their rights.
I have said before in this house, and I repeat, that in my opinion it should never be necessary for any soldier to have to consult his reeve, his mayor, a lawyer, or his member of parliament, in order to prove his case before the pension board and obtain the benefits to which he is entitled. The people of Canada most earnestly desire and expect, I am sure,
The Address-Mr. White

that every member of the armed forces will receive the most careful and most considerate attention in the matter of pension allowances.
I would like to concur in the proposal made last week by the horn, member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), that any changes in legislation, or any new regulations affecting the welfare of soldiers or their dependents, should not be instituted by order in council but should be brought before this house for discussion and debate. The new regulations announced a week ago by the minister illustrate the importance of this suggestion, because they will affect the welfare of many thousands of soldiers. Surely this change is of enough importance to be brought before the house.
While some changes for the better have been made, there are still many points to which soldiers object. I would draw the attention of the house to two letters which have appeared in the press throughout Canada, one written by Everett Bristol, district commander of the Canadian Legion, the other by Mr. Williamson, dominion secretary of the Canadian Corps Association, and I wish to quote very briefly from them. In Mr. Bristol's letter he states:
In addition to unfair discrimination against officers, there are other unsatisfactory features in the new regulations. For example, only those who qualify for the increased hospital allowances whose treatment is "continued without interruption from the date of discharge from the armed forces."
This may mean that if an officer or man discharged from hospital as fit or on pension has a relapse within a few weeks and has to go back for prolonged further treatment, he will get only hospital allowances instead of and lower than his service pay.
Further, the new hospital allowances may be continued only for a period equalling that of the man's service or for twelve months following discharge from the forces, whichever is lesser. What has length of service to do with a disability incurred on service? A man may get badly injured early in his training and require months of hospitalization. Surely he is not to be discriminated against unless there has been misconduct on his part.
I quote from the letter by Mr. Williamson:
In its opinion, no officer or man should be discharged from the service until he has been released from hospital to return to civilian life. Less than this is unworthy of this country and detrimental in the extreme to morale in all the services. Any person disabled by reason of military service should be retained on the strength until his period of treatment is concluded. If, as will be the case with a small minority, men are confined to a hospital bed for the balance of their lives, these men should be encouraged to feel that Canada is mindful of their welfare as long as they shall live. The cheese-paring implication that, after one year, they are to be forgotten will not do.
The minister will be the first one to admit that these provisions, while they correct and
IMr. White.]
improve many of the conditions, are still far from what they should be, and I think he will agree that any soldier suffering any injury is entitled to hospital treatment until he is fully restored to health.
When the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) speaks I should like him to explain to the house the present and future role of the reserve army in Canada. There is no doubt the reserve army has played a very important part in obtaining recruits for the armed forces. The cost of the reserve army must run into many hundreds of thousands a year and the minister should explain how this very large expenditure is justified. He should explain also the present and future role of the home defence army in Canada. This army, whose numbers are between 80,000 and 100,000, is maintained solely for the defence of Canada, and I think everyone is most anxious to know whether or not these men are to be made available for service anywhere in the world. Other hon. members have raised the same point, and the time is long past when the people of Canada are entitled to a public declaration by the government as to the future role of the home defence army; for if these men are to remain in Canada, what is the advantage of continuing to call men for service? To-day men are being called from the farms; schoolboys are being called, as well as men from industry and from the small businesses. Why put these young men into the army if they are to serve only in Canada? The cost of the home defence army must run into hundreds of millions a year, and I hope that the minister will justify this large expenditure if it is the intention of the government to keep these men in Canada. If they are to remain in this country, what was the object of the plebiscite vote? Is the government still afraid of the "no" majority given in the province of Quebec? What about the matter of reinforcements for troops in England? The Minister of National Defence should give the house a very frank and complete statement on the question of reinforcements for the troops in England. To-day, with the invasion hour drawing nigh, there will be great need of many reinforcements, and if the minister feels that the matter cannot be discussed in public, let him tell the members in 3ecret session. What an opportunity to have General McNaughton present-the man who knows more about the matter of reinforcements than anyone else! All members of the house, as well as the citizens of Canada, are entitled to this information.
Let me mention briefly the two tables that appear in "Canada at War," January, 1944, and January, 1943. These tables set out the per-

The Address-Mr. White
centage of enlistments in the three branches of the armed services and also show the number called up under the National Resources Mobilization Act. It is the same old story of eight provinces making more than a fair and equal contribution of men to the armed forces and the ninth province lagging behind. An examination of the tables will show the truth of this statement. I would ask the government if this is what it considers equality of service. In fact, I think there is grave doubt about the matter, if the figures in this table are correct, as pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he spoke on Friday last.
I would ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell), with reference to military district No. 5, whether young men are not called until they reach the age of nineteen. If this is not correct, then I think the Minister of Labour should explain to the house how the difference in figures is accounted for, because in January, 1943, the male population was shown as 214,300 between the ages of nineteen and forty-five, and yet one year later, when the eighteen year olds are included, it is shown as 214,000. If they are called when they are eighteen the minister should so inform us-or are they not called until they are nineteen? Would the Minister of Labour also amplify the statement he read to the house this afternoon in which he said that some 3,500 men from the province of Quebec had been given permits to cross the border and work in the New England states. This is the first time, to my knowledge, that we have had such a great surplus of manpower in Canada that 3,500 men from one province could cross the line to work in the New England states. It might be interesting to know how many of the 3,500 are of military age and also how many work permits have been granted to men in the other provinces permitting them to cross the line in order to work in the United States.
I concur in what has been said by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson), the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) with regard to the new wage order, P.C. 9384, which has given rise to so much controversy. This new wage order was well analysed by the hon. member for York West, who indicated the grave injustices that are being done to labour in particular from the point of view of appeals and the onus of proof. I am amazed that the cabinet should pass such an order. Where is their sense of fair play or British justice when an order- is passed which takes away rights which have existed for every British citizen from the time that magna charts was signed at Runnymede?
Surely it is well established in British jurisprudence that every citizen has the right of appeal to the highest court in the land. When has the new doctrine come into being in this country that a man must prove himself innocent? Why is it necessary to write into any statute or any order in Canada that the benefit of the doubt is not to be given to the accused? I think every hon. member has a duty to rise and protest against this infringement of rights which has existed for so many years. I, for one, should like the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) to explain to hon. members why it was necessary in the fifth year of the war to insert any such clause in any order in Canada. Surely the day is never going to come in this country when the right to appeal to the court or the right of a citizen to be presumed innocent until proven guilty is to be taken away. The inclusion of any such restrictive regulation as that smacks of the gestapo of Germany.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to emphasize the following points for the attention of the government:
1.	A long furlough for all soldiers on discharge with full pay and allowances.
2.	No member of the armed forces to be discharged without being provided with a suitable job.
3.	A speeding up in the handling of pension applications.
4.	Clothing allowance to be increased from S65 on a sliding scale and made retroactive.
5.	The insurance principle to be reinserted in the Pension Act.
6.	The provisions of the Pension Act to apply to all soldiers injured on leave in Canada, and a review made of all such cases.
7.	Soldiers to have all necessary hospital treatment irrespective of the length of service.
8.	Rehabilitation grant to be increased and made retroactive to cover all soldiers discharged to date.
9.	That the widow of a soldier who had a pension disability of less than fifty per cent be granted a pension after the death of her husband.
10.	Dependent's allowance to a mother to be on the same scale as now payable to a wife.
11.	That a review be made by the pension commission of all soldiers suffering from shell shock, mental or nervous cases where no pension has been granted.
12.	That the onus of proving that the disability was incurred or due to war service be on the pension commission.

The Address-Mr. Shaw

13.	That a committee of this house be appointed to review scale of pensions to members of the armed forces, pensions to widows, dependents' allowances, clothing allowances, mustering-out pay and all other matters affecting the welfare of the soldier or his dependents.
14.	That the Minister of National Defence tell this house whether or not the members of the home defence army are to be made available for service anywhere in the world.
15.	The introduction of a system of calling men for military service whereby all parts of Canada will make an equal and fair contribution.
16.	That no policy of immigration be undertaken until such time as proper provision has been made for full-time jobs and the complete reestablishment and rehabilitation of all members of the armed forces and all other Canadian workers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the commencement of the present session of parliament and upon several occasions during the debate which is now taking place reference has been made to the fact that the members are engaging too extensively in debate. It would appear to me that there is a definite tendency, or probably I should say a definite effort from some quarters, further to deprive the private members of this house of the opportunity of giving full expression to their thoughts relative to the many matters that come before the house. How could it be otherwise when the members of this house find it so necessary to occupy so much of their time in debate? Why is it that members of the house should be accused of devoting too much time to matters of little consequence? I have given a good deal of thought to this matter and I find that it is wrapped up largely in the following facts. First, we find throughout this country boards actually legislating, such legislation having the effect of law. These boards deal with the most important matters, matters which, in -my opinion, should be dealt with by parliament. In the second place, the government have perfected a scheme of mass production of orders in council. These orders in council are being passed not only between sessions of parliament but also during the actual time that parliament is in session. I find therefore that we have to devote so much time to dealing with matters regarded by some as of little consequence because the major issues are decided outside this House of Commons.
I am becoming extremely suspicious of any attempt to curtail the rights of the private members of the House of Commons, whether
	,

in connection with debate or in connection with any other matter which may in effect deprive the individual of performing his duties as an elected member of this House of Commons. We find that, this dissatisfaction with respect to the actions of the government is not confined to any small group in this house, nor is it confined to any particular cross-section of opinion in this house, because this afternoon an hon. member asserted that two members of the Liberal party during the past two days expressed what I would call almost absolute disgust regarding the attitude of the government in failing -to consult members of the house with respect to major matters affecting the country.
In referring to the speech from the throne, I find that emphasis is laid upon the fact that the winning of the war clearly remains the first of all our objectives. With that statement there is no possibility of disagreement. We are as one, I am sure, in that objective. Canadians who still have their feet, on the ground and their heads out of the clouds will recognize that we must continue to exert our utmost energy toward an early and successful termination of hostilities. During the past year much has taken place to give us renewed hope and renewed confidence; yet we are certain as we gaze about into the various theatres of war that the road ahead is bound to be long and bound to be rutted. However, we have confidence in the calibre of the men of our fighting forces. That is reflected from the heroic achievements in the various theatres of war, in Italy, over Europe and elsewhere where they are engaged in conflict. If one reflects upon the decorations that have been awarded during the war he will find that every province in Canada has been represented; he will find that those of the various racial origins within the country are represented, as are also the various creeds. The army on the home front and the civilian population have acquitted themselves most magnificently. I refer to the farmers and to the industrial workers, in fact, to all of those engaged in work associated with the prosecution of the war.
The future, though, will depend largely upon the policies instituted by this government and the -action the government may or may not take in connection with the prosecution of the war and the preparation now for the post-war period. As to both of these matters I shall have something more to say shortly, but at this point I should like to make reference to a'matter which is of extreme concern to me. When fascist Italy was presumed to have capitulated demonstrations took place in many parts of Canada, par-

The Address-Mr. Shaw
ticularly in that part in which I happen to reside. I do not know under whose direction this was done; I do not know who were responsible for making the people in certain quarters think that in effect the war was over, but that was the feeling. Shortly after, however, when our forces were engaged in such mortal conflict on the soil of Italy, the reaction set in. It was a feeling of distress and discouragement. If I recall correctly some of the demonstrations were called off, but others were carried through. Those responsible for causing the people to believe that in effect the war was over should guard against a recurrence of any such error.
The speech from the throne refers to the various social security measures which the government propose to introduce during this session of parliament. It mentions "a national minimum of social security and human welfare," and later, "such a programme contemplates social insurance against privation resulting from old age." Presumably this refers to contributory old age pensions. One encounters extreme difficulty in restraining himself when speaking on this matter of old age pensions, in dealing with the consideration or la>ck of it which is given to thousands of our older people, the pioneer citizens of Canada. As all hon. members are aware, within the boundaries of the dominion we have thousands of worthy citizens in the lower income brackets, many of whom are in receipt of meagre incomes insufficient to provide the necessities of life. They are utterly unable to secure employment, and thus must depend upon one of two things: the hopelessly inadequate pension which they may obtain to-day, provided they can prove themselves paupers or provided they have the ability to conceal the truth; or the charity of friends, relatives or others who may take pity upon them. In my view the present Old Age Pensions Act, which was passed by this parliament, and the regulations related thereto, have stained the statute books of this land long enough. I contend that if we are sincere in our promise with respect to social security measures we can prove our good faith by setting out to-day to erase from our statute books the act which now exists, replacing it with one which might be regarded as a Christian act, or by so amending it as to make adequate provision for those people who, all hon. members of this house will agree, at least in private, are deserving of more consideration than they are receiving at the present time. The rates of pension established in 1928 bore no relation at all to the cost-of-living index of that day, nor have they borne such relation at any time since. As I indicated a moment ago, 100-161
a person who has reached seventy years of age and is able to prove himself a pauper or who' has the ability to conceal the truth, may qualify for the pittance we now offer. It is then charged against property owned at five per cent compound interest.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, I can have no faith in the intentions of any government until such time as the conditions now prevailing are rectified. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) is very well aware of these conditions. On one occasion he said that the war had not banished suffering from this land. On another occasion he said that we could not put forth our utmost strength if we neglected the elementary human needs of the unfortunate and the suffering in our midst. On another occasion he said that the people of this country were committed to the utmost of our strength to the cause of humanity in its hour of greatest peril, and then he declared that we could not afford to forget claims equally pressing upon our generosity and upon our social and individual consciousness. In the light of that; in the light of what we all know is absolutely true, I say we should immediately take the steps necessary in connection with this matter.
Then the speech from the throne says:
While giving to the needs of the war precedence over all else, my ministers are resolved .that, so far as the future can be foreseen, Canada will be in a position to meet the difficult situations which will have to be faced when victory is won.
I assume this refers specifically to our postwar relationships with both allied and nonallied nations of to-day. In my humble judgment Canada stands destined to play a most important role in shaping. post-war world relationships. Moreover, I think our success or failure in the role that we shall be certainly called upon to play will depend entirely upon the calibre and motives of the men who speak and act for Canada. The task will not be an easy one; we all know that. But the experiences of the past few decades do cast a most ominous shadow over the future; one need not be a pessimist to realize this. We have fought wars in the past, and each has been more costly and more devastating than the one which preceded it. Between major military wars, minor military wars have been fought; and while those military wars were being fought, and in between them, economic warfare was carried on. I charge that the effects of the economic warfare have been just as devastating as those of military warfare, and in no small way responsible for such warfare. These boys of ours who are fighting on the blood-soaked soil of Italy or who are facing danger over
The Address-Mr. Shaw

Europe to-day and every day are fighting, it is said, to preserve our democratic institutions and the integrity of the British commonwealth. Others say they are fighting in the hope that after the war will come an opportunity for reestablishment in a land free from war. Third, it is said that they are fighting in the expectation that their sons will not have to pay the supreme sacrifice twenty years hence. I am inclined to believe that we should bear all three of these in mind when considering post-war matters. In referring to the returned soldiers, the speech from the throne states:
A broad programme has already been developed for the reestablishment of veterans of the present war, and for the care of disabled veterans and the dependents of our fighting .men and merchant seamen.
Then it goes on to state that gratuities will ibe paid to these men of the service. I think .all the people of Canada are of one mind as to the men of our fighting forces and the *debt of gratitude, transcending any other debt claim which may arise from this war, that we owe to them. We know that the men of our fighting forces are looking to *the people at home to see that we make this country worthy of their magnificent courage and unstinting sacrifice and of the ideals for which they are fighting. The carrying out of this obligation rests squarely upon and is the responsibility of all the people of Canada. It is a vital aspect of Canada's war effort, and therefore I find it utterly impossible to agree with those who assert that during the actual prosecution of the war we should be devoting no time to the consideration of and preparation for the post-wax period.
In referring to the treatment that we are now according the soldiers who have returned from overseas, may I say that I have been filled with alarm over the fact that many of those soldiers who have come home from the theatres of war have not been given their just desserts. I know that as far as my home district is concerned, too many of these men are having to go to their member of parliament in order to secure what most of them refer to as simple justice. Hon. members who have preceded me have referred to the matter of physical examinations. The speaker who iust preceded me indicated that the examinations preceding enlistment are thorough. I am not going to challenge his statement; I am simply going to say that many of the cases which have come to my attention in western Canada have proven the contrary to be the case.	'
For instance, a lad proceeds to a recruiting depot and is directed to those whose duty it is to give him a physical examination. In a

number of cases that have come to my attention the lads have referred to disabilities which were incurred as youngsters, and yet they were categorized as "Al". Later on, following discharge, a lad would be told that his disability is not attributable to or aggravated by war service, that his trouble was due to the disability he had had before. Therefore he cannot secure pension. I contend in all sincerity that if a man is examined as thoroughly as it is indicated he is and is placed in "Al" category and comes out an "E" category man, it is only fair to conclude that his disability was attributable to or aggravated by his war service.
I wonder too about the examinations given to men who are moved from one depot to another, one examination being given before they leave the one place and the other after they arrive at their destination. Being from the west, I find it difficult to use language that would convey to the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) what the boys in uniform call that type of examination. Some time I hope to be able to give a description of it to him in person.
