I should like to refer to some of the cases where men have been injured, let us say while in the performance of duty in the British isles. I will refer to one case which I believe illustrates the point I am trying to make. A man was injured during commando practice. His injuries to his lower abdomen were so severe that it was necessary for his comrades to carry him back from where they were carrying on manoeuvres. He was hospitalized for a lengthy period of time; he was shifted from one hospital to another and was examined by one medical board after another. His disability was diagnosed as being three or four different things. In one instance they called it ulcers of the stomach, but they neglected to add that his stomach had fallen because his disability was low in the abdomen. They had him ready for operation, but shortly before the operation was to be performed they moved him out of the hospital in anticipation of Dieppe casualties arriving, it being just at that time. After he had been moved about for approximately three months he was sent home to Canada to be discharged. Before discharge they confined him in the neurological ward of a certain hospital in Quebec and then discharged him with depressive psychosis, not

The Address-Mr. Shaw
pensionable. I have no doubt that if any hon. member of this house received treatment of that kind following an injury he would have a disability far more serious than depressive psychosis. .If this man has that, the government is responsible.

My hon. friend says, "Maybe the government has it." That's possible. There are too many such cases. I refer to one other case. This man went through the Dieppe raid and received a bullet in his spine. He was decorated because even with that bullet in his spine he carried an officer out of the field of battle. He was sent back to Canada to be discharged. He was kept in military district 13, Calgary, for almost a month, until they could find out what they were going to do with him. One day he was paraded before the medical officer who was seated behind a desk. The medical officer asked him how he felt. Most of us in the west say that we feel fine whether we do or not. After a few moments of conversation he was handed a paper. When he walked out of the office and looked at it he found that he was recategorized as "A 1" to be sent back overseas. He got as far as Debert before a friend of his, a captain in the medical corp, discovered him and asked what he was doing there. He told him he was on his way back to England. That young captain prevented his being moved on. He was held there a month, discharged on the spot and told to discover some method by which he could get home.
I am not blaming the minister for these things, but I sometimes wonder what check there is upon some of these individuals who are responsible for cases like these. Why is it that the bulk of the cases I take to the Minister of Pensions and National health are reopened and either higher pensions granted or a pension granted where none was given before? Does that not indicate to the minister that there must be something wrong with the whole system?

I would hardly say that. I must say in all fairness that he has been very fair as far as I am concerned. It should not be necessary to bring up such matters as these in this house, but as far as I am concerned these cases are coming much too frequently. Out of those who have come home to my community, too many have had to come to me to have their cases taken up. I presume
there are others who did not come to me but endeavoured to secure justice from other-quarters.
I wish now to refer to the Progressive Conservative amendment. The first clause (a) refers to the failure of the government "to make adequate - provision and to implement promises already made for the immediate needs and employment of the men and women of the armed forces on demobilization." I find myself in a position where I must agree with that. I feel that the government has not done more than enact a measure here and a measure there; it has not laid down any concrete over-all policy to meet the over-all problem which will confront the country upon demobilization. Many existing measures are inadequate. The amendment goes on in paragraph (b) to say:
(b)	Failed to provide adequate measures-whereby agriculture can make its maximum war and peace-time contribution through a stable and effective long-term programme.
There can be absolutely no disagreement with that. I wonder why it has not been possible for this government to do more than adopt a very short-range policy in connection! with agriculture. For instance, in my part of Alberta last fall a serious situation, developed with respect to hogs. Due to hail and frost feed shortages existed. It was extremely difficult for them to purchase feed at the prices prevailing. Hog prices fell. Farmers immediately set about to dispose of their breeding stocks. Liquidation took place which has impaired the potential hog production, and I contend that it will be years before the hog producers of areas in the Red Deer constituency will be able to recover the loss which was sustained when they found it essential to dispose of their sows.
Then paragraph (c) of the Progressive Conservative amendment states:
(c)	Failed to establish such a national! code for labour as will ensure maximum production and give to labour its rightful place in our national partnership; and failed to provide for the correction of the unfairly coercive and restrictive clauses in the 1943 wartime wages control order;
I doubt if there is a private member of the house who will disagree with the sentiment there expressed. That wage order has been, discussed in this house by many hon. members-since the debate began, and I agree with what the amendment states. I vehemently disagree with the order that was passed'.
Then (d):
(d)	Failed to lessen bureaucratic controls and regimentation and to recognize and restore the supremacy of parliament; and failed to halt the continuing infringement of provincial rights-and the centralization of authority.
The Address-Mr. Shaw

I wonder if Mr. John Bracken has changed his ideas with respect to the Sirois recommendations. Nothing within my memory has been presented in Canada that so seriously threatened the autonomy of the provinces of Canada as did the recommendations of the Sirois report.

I now come to the amendment to the amendment. I would hardly care to try to convey the impression that by moving to *strike out the whole Progressive Conservative amendment the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party are in disagreement with it all, and I am not going so to charge. The C.C.F. party say in their amendment:
We respectfully submit to Your Exeelleney that in the opinion of this house Your Excellency's advisers have failed to propose the fundamental social changes and economic planning which alone can hasten the winning of the war and make possible the establishment of a post-War Canada capable of providing full employment and complete social security.
I am confounded by that wording; I wonder what it means. The expression "fundamental social changes" may mean anything. It refers to .planning. What type of planning? I wonder that the C.C.F. party did not strike out 'both those expressions and put in "socialism". Why did they not do so? The issue would then have been clear. I have reason to believe that there may have been a good reason for not doing so. When it comes to determining the value of that amendment I must make a decision in the light of what has gone before and in the light of the interpretations that may be put upon a vote one way or the other after the subamendment has been voted on. During the past three months I have become more suspicious, particularly in view of the assertions made by the leader' of the C.C.F. party during the byelection in Red Deer, in Alberta.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What did he say?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I was so incensed, Mr. Speaker, by what he said that I might have to refer to two or three of his statements. In fact, my people would consider it strange if I did not do so, because, after all, here was the leader of a national party who came into a provincial by-election in Alberta and made the most startling assertions, so startling that I could hardly credit them to him. One of them was that the C.C.F. party was the only party in the House of Commons which had protested against the shipment of scrap iron to Japan. He also said that his was the only party which had opposed the present financial monopoly. His was the only party, he also said, which had consistently opposed fascism. He also said that his was the only party which had a programme which comes out of the people. Then, to cap the whole thing, he asserted that the government of Alberta had given away the resources of the province to private monopoly and corporations; but when he was asked to name one he said, "I am not in a position to know what the government of Alberta has or has not done." I would not accept those statements, if they were merely hearsay, but I drove into the city of Red Deer one night during the campaign and parked my car across from the Crescent theatre and heard the hon. gentleman's voice coming over the loud speaker. As I sat there I took notes. I heard these statements. Others sat with me in the car and heard. So it is not hearsay; it is facts. I say to the members of the C.C.F. party that I deplore that sort of thing. I have always tried to be perfectly fair, and I have not made assertions unless I am reasonably certain that they are correct and that I can support them.

speechtext:
In supporting the C.C.F.
amendment I am not supporting socialism, that is bureaucratic planning.
In the speech from the throne reference is made to the question of foreign trade. That is, to exports and imports. I have given considerable thought to this particular aspect of our national life because, after all, foreign trade has occupied in the past a dominant position in the life of this country. Exports, tariffs and exchanges have caused governments headaches or have been the major worry of governments for decades. Thus far, difficulties have developed with respect to foreign trade because governments have endeavoured to carry on a foreign trade policy by stimulating production within the country, increasing exports from the country, and at the same time erecting tariff barriers to keep the produce of other countries out of Canada. All the while the vain hope existed that unemployment would in some miraculous way cease to exist. Most nations were engaged in an almost identical policy, that of endeavouring to stimulate production by exporting and at the same time erecting tariff barriers to keep out the produce of other countries. We all know that the result has been the most bitter type of economic warfare which the world has ever witnessed, and one which has played no small part in the developments of military warfare, in one of which wars we are at present engaged. While these governments were so endeavouring to export and refuse to import, we witnessed the international discount houses rendering the situation far more difficult by the manipulation of exchanges. We must pray that when this war is over, and even before it is over, as the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has so often suggested, our first major concern will be the creating of an effective demand against our own production, exporting surplus production in exchange 'or the goods of other countries, goods which we may require and can buy and the elimination of the policy which we have been following in the past will do much toward preventing a recurrence of the conditions of war which confront us at the present time.
I had hoped to expand this topic, but I understand that my time has elapsed.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like my first word to be one of congratulation to the mover (Mr. Tremblay) and the seconder (Mr. Tucker) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Of the hon. member who moved the address, I can say that he lived up to the high traditions of his race; of the hon. member who seconded it, that he upheld the splendid reputation which he has built up for himself during the past few years.
I know that the last speaker will pardon me if in my few remarks I do not follow his arguments. He seemed to pick out a few individual cases in an attempt to build up a case against the government, without giving the government credit for the many good works it has done. But probably he was on sounder ground even there than he would have been had he attempted to expound the theories of his group. Hon. members in that section of the house are very sincere types, preachers and teachers, rather critical, but lacking practical experience, and for that reason we from the maritimes cannot follow their strange philosophies.
The speech from the throne, as is right and proper, puts first things first. It refers first to the war, which after all is our main concern, because if we do not win the war there is little good in our planning for the future.
Taking an over-all picture of the war effort of this government, I cannot but feel that each and every Canadian, no matter what his race, creed or political affiliations, must recognize that it has in every possible way done credit to Canada. It is true that some of our people are not taking too kindly to many of the regulations which are of necessity imposed on them. However, as I say, taking a broad view of the matter, I believe that to-day, for the most part, these things are necessary.
In the part of the country from which I come one problem which is staring us in the face is the man-power situation. This situation is such, on account of voluntary enlistments, and of men leaving our province to work in other provinces, or joining the merchant navy, that our pool from which we can draw men for practically any work is now at a very low ebb. I propose to quote one paragraph from a letter from a person who is very close to the national resources mobilization board in our province. He says:
There is no new reservoir to call from now
in this province except as they come of age. This is going to mean that from now on to quite a considerable extent men taken into the forces have got to be culled who previously have had postponements.
The Address-Mr. Purdy

You have only to be engaged in industry in our province to realize how true that statement is. Men are being called up every day and we have no one to take their places. I cannot quite understand why, in our little province, which has been in the lead in voluntary enlistments, we are still called upon to furnish the same percentage of men under the National Resources Mobilization Act as those provinces which have not furnished the same percentage of volunteers. This is a matter that should be given very careful study by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of National Defence, and I respectfully suggest that the time must have arrived when there should be put into force a system that uses the same yardstick across Canada to bring men into the services. In other words, I feel that after more than three years of applying the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act there should be a more general levelling off in the number of men in the services as between one province and another.
I now come to my own constituency. In that constituency we have a population of roughly 52,000; and while I may be a little generous in my calculations, yet, on the basis of several yardsticks which I will mention later on, it seems to me that roughly ten per cent of our total population have joined the forces in one way or another. This is only an estimate, not based on any information from the various departments, since they do not keep records in this manner, but I take three yardsticks from which I shapp attempt to prove my point to some extent. First, in the county of Hants, with a population of 22,000 one of the newspapers, the Hants Journal, has kept a record of the men and women in the service. That list is in excess of 2,000, and it does not take into account the men in the merchant navy. Let me take another method of measurement. A few Sundays ago, in the church which it is my privilege to attend, St. Andrews United church, Truro, an honour roll was un-vieled disclosing 120 names out of 600 adherents. Let me take still another point. The coloured population in Truro numbers 503, and out of that population more than fifty young men have joined the forces. I feel we can find the same situation in any community in the constituency. My point is that our young men and women, irrespective of colour, creed or race, have joined the services in very large numbers, and I am glad to say that practically all are ready and willing to serve anywhere. These young men and women are serving wherever Canadians are in action, and casualties are mounting. Their graves are found in many lands, and there they will rest 
until the great day when they will be joined by their loved ones and their fellow-warriors, whose last resting place is known only to our Creator. Our duty to the loved ones of those who die is clear, as it is to those who are wounded and to their dependents.
The present government has gone a long way in this direction, and I feel that under the wise guidance of our Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) it will continue the good work and improve .our pensions and veterans' allowance legislation.
To those who return in health we also owe a deep debt of gratitude and we must see that the Canada to which they return is a Canada worthy of the high ideals for which they are fighting. They do not want charity. They do not want to be wards of the state. They do not want to be regimented pawns in a socialistic state. They want an opportunity to work and live in a country of free enterprise where initiative will bring its rewards. We must see that they have this opportunity, and as long as I am a member I pledge my efforts along these lines and trust that the government will lose no time in bringing in the necessary legislation.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that in the days of ancient Rome when Horatius kept the bridge he was rewarded, together with his fellow-warriors, and Macaulay has commemorated it in the following lines:
They gave him of the corn-land,
That was of public right,
As much as two strong oxen ,
Could plow from morn till night;
And they made a molten image,
And set it up on high,
And there it stands unto this day To witness if I lie.
In this enlightened age we cannot do less; indeed, we must do more for our enlisted forces.
I will now deal for a few minutes with the peace-time programme outlined in the speech. Coming from the maritime provinces, I shall no doubt be expected to raise the cry of maritime rights. You have not heard much of this in the last few years, but I will say that while that cry has been allowed to rest during the war it is not dead. Perhaps you will expect me, coming as I do from the little province of Nova Scotia, to speak of ships and sailormen, of the present-day equivalent of the wooden ships and iron men of confederation days, or of fish and fishermen. The land of which I am now speaking is referred to by another poet, Bliss Carman, in these lines:	'

The Address-Mr. Purdy
The tides go out, the tides come in,
With the breath of the living sea.
And what will they take in trade again From the ports of Acadie?
The freshening wind and the saving salt They bring from the outer vast,
To mould and quicken the men they need To serve their Lord at last.
Then get you down to the sea, my lads,
And go you forth, my dears,
You have reaped the tide, you must sow the tide,
As it was these thousand years.
Certainly in this crisis our young men have gone down to the sea wherever the opportunity has presented itself. However, I will not speak of these activities of our province. I will leave it to members who are better qualified to speak on ships and shipping. I do wish, however, to take as my text this evening-perhaps you think I am going into the poets-a few lines from Longfellow's "Evangeline":
Giving the village its name, and pasture to flocks without number.
Dikes, that the hands of the farmers had raised with labour incessant,
Shut out the turbulent tides; but at stated seasons the flood-gates
Opened, and welcomed the sea to wander at will o'er the meadows.
West and south there were fields of flax, and orchards and cornfields
Spreading afar and unfenced o'er the plain; and away to the northward
Blomidon rose, and the forests old, and aloft on the mountains-
And then along a little further:
Late, with the rising moon, returned the wains from the marshes,
Laden with briny hay that filled the air'with its odour.
I quoted that, Mr. Speaker, because I wish to refer to the marsh-lands of Nova Scotia, and this is my introduction. My constituency has over a hundred and fifty miles of shore along the Cobequid bay and Minas basin. This country was settled by the Acadians and is very close to the village of Grand Pre made famous by Longfellow's poem. We have splendid farming lands in the valleys of the rivers running into this bay and into Minas basin and also into Northumberland strait. I make this explanation because it is often thought we have in Nova Scotia very poor agricultural land. However, we must remember that the lands I have referred to were settled back in 1655 and have been producing crops for more than three hundred years. Where the dykes have been kept up and the ground properly looked after there is no sign of the crops lessening. I give that explanation because we often hear of areas in the west subject to soil drifting where there have been
crop failures following a few years of cultivation.
What I should like to propose to-night is a five-year plan for the rehabilitation of agriculture in Nova Scotia. It is true it is an ambitious programme ; however, I think it is a programme that would produce excellent results. I break this programme into six parts. Much has been said in this house with respect to our marsh-lands. My proposal would be to expend $200,000 a year for five years to bring our marsh-lands back into a productive state. I would propose a further expenditure of $150,000 a year for five years to build up a system of small abattoirs and cold storage plants situated at various points throughout the province. At the present time we have no abattoir and very few cold storage plants. Any slaughterings that are to be marketed under government inspection must be done outside the province.
I come now to another item of $100,000 for five years to control flood conditions on our streams. The rush of waters in the past years, brought about to some extent by heavy timber cuttings on our mountains, has destroyed hundreds and hundreds of acres of splendid land. I would propose the expenditure of $50,000 a year for five years to eneour age the raising of sheep in our little province. Textile experts in the town of Truro tell me that Nova Scotia wool is the best they can get anywhere for the work they have to carry on. They tell me that the fleece is heavier than the fleeces of sheep produced in other sections, and that the wool is stronger. Nova Scotia lamb requires no words of mine to advertise it because it has a market in the United States, in Ontario and in Quebec; in fact there is a great demand for it. I would propose $50,000 a year for five years be spent to bring our people into the growing of flax. I was talking to two experts from the federal Department of Agriculture and they say they have in their possession wonderful linen made from flax grown in Nova Scotia. May I refer again to experts from the textile mills in my constituency. They tell me that the soil and the climate of Nova Scotia are excellent for this class of agriculture. I have one more suggestion to offer and it is in regard to our farm woodlots. Many of our farmers have wood-lots adjoining their farms. In the old days they would sell their timber en bloc; an operator would come in; he would cut what was on the woodlot, and it was fifty or sixty years before the farmers got another crop. My idea is that we should spend $50,000 a year for five years to teach our farmers how to crop their woodlots. That would give them
The Address-Mr. Purdy

a steady income each year instead of a few thousand dollars one year and nothing in the next fifty years.
This programme is, as I, said, rather ambitious. I suggest the expenditure of $3,000,000 in Nova Scotia extending over a period of five, years. However, that is very, verj small when we compare it with the expenditure made on agriculture in western Canada. We have no objections to that in Nova Scotia, but we think our farmers should be given the same treatment. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act there has been over $16,000,000 spent in the past eight years, an average of something over $2,000,000 a year. If that was the only claim I had in asking for this $3,000,000 for my province, perhaps I would not feel satisfied that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), who comes from down our way and keeps of course very close watch upon the purse-strings, would give it to us; but I propose to try to show to the minister that under our present system of taxation we would only be getting back what we are paying in. Under the dominion-provincial agreements, income tax and certain corporation taxes have been taken away from the provinces in an effort to level out the tax structure in the various provinces.
I will attempt to show that under our present system we in Nova Scotia are contributing a greater proportion of the taxes than are some of the other provinces. In other words, if we could obtain $600,000 a year for five years we would, under the present differential in taxafion, be getting back only what we are paying into the federal treasury in excess of some of the other provinces. That seems like a big statement. To prove my point I shall mention first the sales tax on electrical enegry. That tax is only eight per cent, it is true, but it is based on the dollar amount of the bill; and with electrical energy in Nova Scotia costing twice as much as it does in most Ontario towns it means that the ordinary individual in my province pays some twenty cents a month or $2.40 a year more than he would pay for the same amount of electrical energy in Ontario. Assuming that we have sixty or seventy thousand outlets, that would mean somehting like $150,000 a year to begin with. Then I have something else to add. Under the dominion-provincial agreements the gasoline tax was guaranteed to the various provinces at a fixed rate. In Nova Scotia w;e imposed a very high gasoline tax as well as a very high licence fee for motor vehicles in lieu of income tax. Our good friends in Ontario and the other provinces were very fortunate. It is true that they had

a personal income tax, but they did not have as high a gasoline tax, nor did they have to pay as much for their automobile licences. Here are just two examples. In Nova Scotia the annual licence fee for a Chevrolet coupe is $20.09. In Ontario I could licence that car for $7. For a two-ton truck, licensed for 16,000 pounds, the fee in Nova Scotia is $152, and in Ontario, $17.50. In Nova Scotia the gasoline tax is ten cents a gallon; in Ontario it is eight cents. That differential may be all right in the case of companies which are allowed to deduct these taxes before they file their income tax return, but think of the position-of an ordinary person like a member of parliament or a salaried individual. He must pay a greater tax on electrical energy; he must pay a greater licence fee for his car and more for his gasoline. At a rough estimate I would say that in filing our income tax returns we are probably at a disadvantage of some $40 or $50 a year in non-deductible items, as compared with Ontario.
There is another item in connection with w'hich I believe the federal government has guaranteed provincial revenues; that is, in revenue from liquor sales. In Nova Scotia, again in order to avoid personal income tax, we had a higher rate of provincial profit on liquor sales. To-day I am told that for a twenty-six ounce bottle of a fair brand of Scotch an individual in Nova Scotia must pay eighty-five cents more than he would in Ontario. If he buys two bottles a month he would be worse off to the extent of $1.70 a month or approximately $20 a year than his opposite number in Ontario; and again that is an item which is not deductible from the income tax. So I say that if we should figure out these various items we would find that the little province of Nova Scotia, under these differentials as compared with the big province of Ontario, is contributing enough to the federal treasury to permit the Minister of Finance to refund that $600,000 a year for five years, and I hope he will take that suggestion under advisement.
I am only a very ordinary individual, Mr. Speaker. I do not claim to represent the people of Canada as a whole, but from time to time I try to present the views and rights of my constituents to the house and the various members of the cabinet. If in so doing I sometimes run contrary to the ideas of the government, that is my misfortune. Nevertheless I act on conviction, which in my opinion is the only basis upon which a true democracy can exist.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate

The Address-Mr. Wright
I should like first to compliment the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I hope that in their caucuses and their councils they will endeavour to see that the government bring down measures which are adequate with respect to the matters mentioned in that speech. Too often the speech from the throne has been like the advance billing for the circus which used to come to my town every year when I was a boy. That billing promised great things, but the performance seldom lived up to the advance notices. I hope the legislation brought down by the government to implement the speech from the throne will be adequate. If it is, the government may Test assured that they will receive the support not only of their own party but of all parties in this house. However, if it brings in only palliatives or half-way measures, then it will receive the criticism which it deserves.
In the speech from the throne the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) indicated that this might be the most serious year of the war as far as our effort is concerned, that we might expect more casualties this year than in the preceding four years of this conflict. I believe that to be so; I think the fighting in Italy would indicate that this is a probability. I do not propose to-night to deal with our war effort; I believe that can be dealt with better after we have heard the ministers of the various war departments and have their programme before us. However, I should like to deg.1 with one matter mentioned in the speech from the throne; that is, the setting up of a department of veterans' affairs. I believe this is a measure which will receive support from all sides of the house. Up to the present time there appears to have been a great deal of confusion among the men discharged from the army. Unless they were sent direct to the Department of Pensions and National Health apparently they had no idea of the various measures which had been provided for their rehabilitation, and as a consequence we as members of this house had them coming to us for information which they should have been given before discharge. When this new department is set up I would hope that the files of all men discharged will be transferred to it, and that the department will see that this information *is available to the men in order that proper use may be made of it.
One matter to which I believe the department should give attention is the setting up of convalescent homes for our soldiers whose injuries are not such that they require hospitalization, Our hospitals are going to be crowded, and many cases could be dealt with
in convalescent homes. Just recently I had a case brought to my attention. This man served three years in the last war, enlisted during the first months of this war and served two years, one of which was overseas. While over there he had a hemorrhage as a result of stomach ulcers and was sent back to Canada. He was sent to the pension board and his disability was indicated as thirty per cent, six per cent due to war service, and he was given a pension of S3.70 a month. He returned home and began working in the local creamery, but after two months work he had another hemorrhage. The local doctor told him it would be necessary to have six months complete rest on a special diet before he would be fit to work again. This man has a wife and two children and he is expected to take six months rest with no worry on $3.70 a month.
There should be convalescent homes to take care of cases like this where men could be sent on full pay and allowance until they were ready to again take their places in civilian life. There will be a number of nervous cases from this war. The strain on men in the air force and in the other mechanized units of our army is much greater than it was during the last war, and there should be some place where these men could be sent to have a real rest among congenial surroundings until they are able to take their place in civilian life. I suggest that the department of veterans' affairs make an effort to establish convalescent homes in Canada immediately.
Another matter with respect to our army to which I should like to refer is that of the home defence army. Many hon. members have referred to this and I must say that I agree with them. We have some 80,000 men in this army who are not available for overseas service, and this at a time when the war has changed from a defensive to an offensive war. This condition does not make common sense. These men should either be available for overseas service or be given their discharge and made available for useful service in civilian life. I suggest that if they are given their discharge they should automatically go into the reserve army so that they would continue to receive part-time training and the authorities would know exactly where they are should they be needed again. There are several industries in Canada where man-power is needed. Agriculture certainly needs more men, so does lumbering and our pulpwood industry. Unless these men are to be available for overseas service I contend they could contribute more to our war effort in civilian life than they are doing to-day.
The Address-Mr. Wright

To-night I propose to deal mainly with agricultural subjects. There is very little with respect to agriculture contained in the speech from the throne, the Qnly mention being the intention to establish floor prices for agricultural products. I think most of us will agree with that; I only hope that the floor is not so full of trap-doors that most farmers in this country will find themselves in the cellar before two or three years have passed. That is the kind of policy this government has had in connection with agriculture ever since the beginning of the war. It has been a minimum policy.
The only advance there has been in prices of agricultural products has occurred after organized agriculture has made a definite fight. That is what happened with respect to butter prices. It was only after the organized agriculturists of this country had put up a tremendous fight that we got any advance in butter prices. The same with beef prices and again with grain prices. Hon. members from all sides of the house have endeavoured to direct the attention of the government to the prices being paid for grain in western Canada and to the fact that they were entirely inadequate. Large delegations came here from western Canada to place these matters before the government, but no action was taken until this fall. Apparently two by-elections in western Canada had more influence on the government than all the rest of the members. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) and the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Burton) upon having done more for the farmers of western Canada than we had been able to do in the four years previous.
I do not like the phrase "floor prices"; I would rather call them "basic prices". Any price that is established for agricultural products must take certain essential things into consideration. First, such price must be sufficient to enable the farmer to pay a fair wage to his help and to his wife and family if they have to be used to produce the products which we need during this war. For ten years before the war and for the first three years of this war agricultural prices were at such a level that the farmer in all parts of Canada was able to produce only because he was using the unpaid labour of his wife and family or paying wages to his help which were a disgrace. I hope that in establishing a basic price for agricultural products this matter will be taken into consideration.
Any basic price for agricultural products should be sufficient to enable the farmer to have a decent home and home surroundings.
I have seen sections in many of our cities

where better homes were needed, but I have seen nothing quite as poor as some of the homes in some of our agricultural districts, especially in northern New Brunswick, northern Ontario and northern Saskatchewan. If a thousand of those homes could be placed adjacent to one of our cities there would be such a howl of public opinion raised against them that something would have to be done. However, because they are scattered and very few people see them we have allowed them to exist as a disgrace to this country for the last twenty years. This basic price should be sufficient to permit the farmer to have the necessary electrical equipment and other amenities of life now available to many of his brothers in the city.
This basic price for agricultural products should be sufficient to permit the farmer to have decent educational facilities. Here again I know that if I could bring a thousand of the schools I have seen in agricultural districts and place them adjacent to one of our cities there would be such a howl of public opinion *that something would have to be done. But again, simply because they are scattered throughout the country and few people see them we allow them to exist.
Any basic price established for agricultural products should be such as would provide decent medical attention for the farmer and his family. For the past number of years there has been only a very poor type of medical attention available to the farmer. While it may be partly due to the war, the fact is that there are many districts in Canada where proper medical attention is mot available. Many of' our medical men are now serving in the navy, army and air force. Our country doctors have been the most abused group of people in our dominion. They have travelled for miles over bad roads in all kinds of weather, giving what service they could to our people and very often receiving only from forty to fifty per cent of the worth of their services because of the prices being received for agricultural products. Again I say that in the establishment of a basic price for agricultural products the matter of medical attention should be taken into consideration.
I feel that basic price for agricultural products should be a price that will fluctuate with the cost of production. If it is established as a floor that cannot be variedl, then if the cost of production rises it is no longer a floor but a cellar. So I say that the price should fluctuate with the cost of production.
I feel certain of this, that if we are to have anything like full employment in Canada after the war, we must give to the people of this country the ability to purchase the goods they

The Address-Mr. Wright
need, and I know of no greater market for goods than our agricultural areas. We talk about export markets. Export markets are very fine, and we need them. But our home market, after all, is our greatest market." With twenty-five per cent of our people engaged in agriculture, there you have a tremendous market in satisfying their needs for goods. We need better homes; we need electrification. What would it mean to Canada if instead of ten per cent of our farms having electricity, ninety per cent of them had that boon? What a demand there would be for electrical equipment in Canada 1 It would put thousands of people to work in our factories producing the goods we need on the farm.
Our farm equipment in Canada has also become depleted during the war. To-day it is not modern by any means. If we receive a basic price for agricultural, products we shall be able to modernize our farm equipment, and that will mean employment for thousands more of our people in Canada.
Another matter with which I wish to deal is referred to in the speech from the throne, which states that it is the intention of the government to establish an industrial bank. Apparently the government is going into the banking business. We in this group have stated that we believe in the nationalization of the banking system. But we do not believe in doing it piecemeal as the government proposes to do it. The government proposes in the speech from the throne to establish an industrial bank. If it is going to establish an industrial bank, why not an agricultural bank too? Agriculture needs credit even more than industry does. Agriculture has always paid more for its credit than industry has, from 50 to 100 per cent more, and it will continue to pay more for its credit unless something is done about it. We in this group believe that credit should be made available to agriculture at approximately 24 per cent. This government is borrowing millions for war purposes at 14 per cent, and surely one per cent would be a sufficient charge for the distribution and collection of agricultural credit. So I say that if we are to have an industrial bank, we should also have an agricultural bank, and see that credit is made available to agriculture at a price that agriculture can afford to pay. That bank would extend long-term loans. We in this group believe that, so far as short-term credit is concerned, probably the encouragement of the credit union movement in this country would serve the purpose. Credit unions are growing by leaps and bounds, and
we believe that with proper encouragement they might be able to take care of a large part of the short-term credit needed by agriculture.
If we fail to establish a basic price for agricultural products and to provide credit for our farm industry I am afraid that the ownership of our farms and homes in Canada will pass out of the hands of those who own them and are farming to-day. Very few people realize just how quickly ownership has been passing from the people, in Canada during the last forty years.
I have some statistics here taken from the 1941 census and from the Economic Annalist for October, 1937, with regard to farm tenancy in Canada. They indicate that in Manitoba the drop in farm ownership has been about 25 per cent; in Saskatchewan 45 per cent, in Alberta 34 per cent, in Ontario the percentage is now almost 48 per cent lower than in 1901.
In the matter of urban home ownership we find that over 48 per cent of the homes in Canada are rented; ownership has passed out of the hands of the occupants of these homes. These statistics also indicate that for the rural areas, farm and non-farm, the percentage occupied by tenants in 1941, when the last census was taken, was 24'4; for farm homes alone, 18'8 per cent; and for rural non-farm homes 33 per cent. In urban centres, which includes even villages with less than 1,000 people, 58-8 per cent of the homes were occupied by tenants. In cities of 30,000 and over, two-thirds of the homes were in this category; in cities of 15,000 to 30,000, and smaller centres of 5,000 to 15,000, about 53 per cent. Taking all urban centres of 15,000 and over combined, almost 65 per cent of the homes were occupied by tenants.
I shall not take time to read the figures for all the provinces but I would ask, Mr. Speaker, that with the consent of the house I might be allowed to place these two tables on Hansard because they give a complete picture of home and farm ownership in the Dominion of Canada.

But they are comprehensive, and well worth studying as an indication of a trend which is going on in Canada to-day, a trend which we in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe should be stopped, and which, if our programme is put into effect, definitely will be stopped.
There is one other matter with which I wish to deal, namely the cooperative movement in Canada. We of the C.C.F. believe not only in private ownership of your home, your farm, and your small business, but we believe that another type of ownership which is to be commended in this country is cooperative ownership.

speechtext: No, we are not. I will explain to my hon. friend in a moment the difference between capitalism and cooperation.

speechtext: What about the viewpoint of your colleague in the Ontario house?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. gentlemen will wait to make their speeches until I am through, I shall be delighted.
As I have stated, we believe in the cooperative movement. In Canada that movement has grown by leaps and bounds during the last number of years. I have here statistics which show that In the year 1942 the reported membership of the cooperatives in Canada exceeded half a million., and the aggregate business was over $250,000,000. Reserves and surpluses reached the high point of $46,000,000 and the working capital position showed general improvement. This is according to A. E. Richards, who is head of the extension department. The cooperative movement is, I believe, the only thing we have in Canada to-day which is a real block to the growth of monopoly capitalism, and as such it should be encouraged by any government in this country. The people who are opposed to the cooperative movement to-day are joining forces to try to stop the growth of that movement. I have in my hand a copy of the Maritime Co-operator for February 1 of this year. In it, Professor MacDonald, speaking before the Nova Scotia Credit Union league on January 12 and 13, makes this statement:
In the United States big business had already formed an anti-cooperative league, pooling thousands of dollars in an attempt to smash cooperative enterprise. Similar efforts, he declared, were already gathering strength in Canada advocating a return to unregulated free enterprise, which he called "a system of free exploitation, favouring the ousting of government control."
It is beyond me how any person can in the same breath say that he believes in competition and capitalism and that be believes in cooperation and cooperatives. Such people are either ignorant of the true meaning of cooperation or they are deliberately trying to mislead.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) wished to know the difference between cooperation and capitalism. The cooperative way of doing business is the direct opposite to the competitive way. Cooperation emphasizes service and equality; competition emphasizes profits and special privileges. We need in Canada to-day a dominion cooperative act which will coordinate the cooperative
The Address-Mr. Wright

movements throughout the dominion. We have in many of our provinces fairly good cooperative acts; and I hope that this government will see fit to bring down a cooperative act which will clarify the position of the cooperatives in Canada in many respects, especially in the matter of taxation. At the present time the pools in western Canada are in a position where they do not know whether they are to be taxed on their earnings during the past number of years, and it places them in a serious position, and one which should be clarified at the earliest possible moment. We have in western Canada also the first cooperative oil refinery established anywhere in the world. It has been doing a fine piece of work as far as western Canada is concerned. It was established some eight years ago with a capital of approximately $32,000; and to-day, after eight years of operation, it has assets of a million and a half dollars, and last year did a business worth two and one-quarter million dollars. Not only has that cooperative been able to build up that capital *during this past eight years, but it has reduced the price of petroleum products to the farmer in western Canada to the extent that the savings in one year on one section of land farmed with mechanized equipment are over three hundred dollars, that is compared with what it would have cost the farmer had that refinery not been established. That is a remarkable showing, and our cooperatives should be encouraged in every way possible.
The fourth point which I wish to bring to the attention of the house is the matter of establishing marketing boards in Canada. I believe we should have a dominion marketing act under which we can establish boards for the marketing of various farm products in the dominion, and the act should make it possible that, where sixty to sixty-five per cent of the growers engaged in the production of any particular farm product agree that they should have orderly marketing through the marketing board, it wTould be compulsory for all that product to be marketed through that board. I believe that is the only way in which we shall be able to obtain orderly marketing in the dominion. As long as small groups of people are left free to disturb the orderly marketing of a particular product because they do not agree to go into that marketing board, I do not think we can have orderly marketing. The greatest factor which is operating against the orderly marketing of farm products in Canada to-day is the surpluses which we may have from year to year on account of weather conditions. We often find that, with very small surpluses existing,
fMr. Wright.]
products are dumped on the market by a few people and the market for those products destroyed. I believe that there should be marketing boards controlled by the growers themselves, in conjunction with an export marketing board which would take care of the surpluses which may occur from year to year, and which, after all, we need. We should not draw the line too close in Canada so as not to have a surplus, because we do not know what the weather man has in store for us. This surplus should be taken off the market by the government board and processed and kept as a reserve against years of crop failure, or it should be made available for export to countries where there are deficiencies. In Hot Springs, Virginia, about two months ago, there was a conference with regard to the supply of food to countries in which there are deficiencies, and the surpluses which We may have in Canada from year to year, now that we have dehydrating plans and we know more about quick-freezing, could be processed and made available to these other countries instead of becoming a drug on the market in our own country, thus destroying the price system which may obtain at the time.
I believe also that we should have in Canada a programme whereby we might have a reserve of non-perishable products such as grains against any year of drought or a series of years of drought, and the best place in which such products can be stored is right on the farms where they are grown. Under the present system we are taking these grains and storing them in large terminals hundreds of miles away from where they are grown, and if we should have a drought in Western Canada again, or two or three years of drought, wc might find ourselves in a position where we would be hauling grain again for seed and feed for the farmers. In the United States they have established such a system as I have suggested. They store grain right on the farm. There is no reason why the same thing cannot be done in Canada. If it were done it would be the best insurance we could have against crop failure and it would give a sense of security to the people living on our farms.
We have a modified form of crop insurance in Canada under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. That act has served a very useful purpose ; but unfortunately, like practically everything else the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has had anything to do with, we find that the operation of this scheme has become riddled with political patronage, thereby destroying in part at least its usefulness. I believe that not only should we have crop insurance for western Canada but that this

The Address-Mr. Wright
crop insurance should be made available to any group of growers of any particular agricultural product who want their crops insured. It might very well be made available to our tobacco growers, or our potato or apple growers, and the cost of that insurance should be taken into consideration in the establishing of basic prices for agricultural products in Canada. There is no other line of industry where the cost of insurance is not written into the price of the goods it produces, and that should apply to the insurance of agricultural products. Any basic price established for agricultural products should be a price which has taken into consideration the cost of insurance of that crop. If we had that type - of scheme in Canada it would give more permanency to agriculture.
Another scheme which has been developed by this government and which has been a very good one is the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme in the west. This has been the first attempt by any government on any large scale to rehabilitate land in Canada. No one who has followed the course of land settlement in Canada during the past one hundred years can fail to be saddened by what has taken place.

speechtext: What is wrong with politics anyhow?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Politics as some people play it is not so hot. That scheme should be extended to cover all the western provinces, and there should be set up-in conjunction with it another scheme in the east to cover Ontario and Quebec, and one for the maritime provinces, because there is absolute need of the rehabilitation of farm lands in this country. One hundred years ago our people came to this country and settled in the maritime provinces and Ontario. No direction whatsoever was given them. They took up land wherever the land companies could secure it and sell it to them. Land was cleared that should never have been used for agricultural purposes. The result was that those people were able to live for a few years on those
farms where they established homes, but because the land should never have been used for agricultural purposes they had to abandon those homes.
Travel throughout Ontario and the mari-times and see these places. Every one represents not only an abandoned farm but lost hopes and ambitions on the part of those who settled on them. We allowed people to go to western Canada and there the same process was gone through They settled on land and after a few years found it was worthless as far as agriculture was concerned, and people left the south of the province and came to the north. This is my criticism of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, that people were allowed to come from the south and settle on the same kind of land in the north. I know of thousands of people who have been brought from the south of the province and established in the north and in twenty years from now they will find themselves in exactly the same position as they were in before. The land is not fit for agricultural purposes. We have had land surveys in Saskatchewan and they have served a useful purpose, but the information has not been disseminated with regard to the land and we have allowed lands to be settled which should never have been settled.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the beginning of this session the view seems to prevail that speeches could very well be shortened as much as possible so that contemplated measures might all the sooner be put into execution. I am heartily in accord with that idea, and, as usual, I shall be quite brief in the remarks I wish to make.
At this stage of the proceedings, we must ask ourselves whether it is convenient, in the interest of the Canadian people as a whole and of our constituents, to support generally the policy outlined by the government in the speech from the throne, which we are now considering. For the present, we must confine ourselves to the principles set forth, reserving
The Address-Mr. Lizotte

the right to discuss each measure and to consider each proposition on its merits as soon as the details are communicated to us.
Ever since I have the honour to be a member of this parliament, I have endeavoured to consider in a spirit of honesty and independence all problems in, their true light, andl to approve or disapprove of them conscientiously, outside of all personal or party considerations.
Of course, that is not the best method for avoiding difficulties, but it is the safest way of being at peace with oneself and keeping the confidence of those who have entrusted their interests to us.
Without any further preliminaries, I do not hesitate to state that we should be unfair if we did not congratulate the government, as warmly as we have sometimes opposed certain measures, for the splendid programme they have outlined for the present session of parliament. The proposals -which are being laid before us are so timely that they can seemingly gain the almost- unanimous support of this house. As was to be expected, the government's opponents, wTho are here for the furtherance of opposite political interests, have referred to that programme as an election manifesto, made out on the eve of an, election. Although my experience in politics is by no means lengthy, I quite understand their embarrassment, but I think it is an indication that the ,programme is good, and such as to meet the wishes of the people. If there is no election before the session ends or before those measures are implemented, no one will be able to claim that, this manifesto is nothing but an election promise.
I believe I may say, therefore, that the fate of the government is in its hands and that its future will depend upon the fairness with which it will carry out the proposed measures.
I do not wish, for the time being, to discuss the war programme of the government. I have had numerous occasions of expressing my views in this connection and I still hold to the same views. We are all agreed that it is absolutely necessary to win the war and to hasten victory, but the fact must be borne in mind that after all Canada is a young nation and that she must act in her own interests and according to her own means, leaving older and wealthier nations more directly concerned to follow the same policy.
I shall therefore confine myself to the plans respecting the period of transition and of peace, outlined in the speech from the throne. How shall we assess these plans?
How could we, on, principle, object to the government's plan of increasing our exports by facilitating the exchange of our products

with those of other nations after the war? We have forests, mines, water-power and other natural resources of untold value, which may be used in international trade. The interests of our people demand that we should be prepared to take advantage of these resources in order to anticipate prosperity.
How could we, on principle, object to our country's individual participation in an international organization which will strive to avert future wars, further catastrophes, and promote universal security? Would not such a policy tend to give recognition to the sovereigifty of Canada, a dream which we have so long Cherished?
How could we denounce the putting into effect of certain plans to establish, during the post-war period, a minimum standard of welfare-better food and shelter, social insurance against the hazards of life, setting-up of a national contributory old age pensions scheme on a more generous basis? If we did, it would be tantamount to opposing the new order which has been held out before our eyes and which can only be attained by properly directed social measures.
Who would say that they oppose the setting up of a body intended to supply the credit necessary for the launching of new industrial enterprises, small and medium in size, and to help those already in existence? That will be our greatest need, both in rural and urban centres, if we are to put all our manpower to work after the war.
I should be amazed beyond words if even one member in the house opposed the principle behind a measure which would carry out family allowances. The idea has been under Consideration for the past fifty years in this country, and the time has come for a government to have the courage to identify itself with such a plan and implement it. It must be well understood, however, that these allowances shall be apportioned so as to reward and encourage a high birth-rate and help particularly the many Canadian mothers who did not shrink from filling the cradle over and over again, in accordance with the precept laid down by the Creator: "Be fruitful and multiply". A government which would apply this one measure of family allowances with Christian fairness would find that it has done enough to secure the support of the people and their forgiveness of its past mistakes in the management of public affairs.
I am pleased to see that the government has expressed its intention of setting a minimum price on farm products. For too long has the farmer, king of the universe, been treated as a poor relation. I have never understood why, if the workingman is unde-

The Address-Mr. Lizotte
niably entitled to a fair salary, the farmer should not also have the right to be paid prices just as fair and reasonable for his products. Because the farmer, who is a peaceful and orderly man, has never cared to resort to force in order to press his claims, he has had to muddle through as best he could until now, and it seemed as if he would remain in a class where the income could not budge. If the government carries out its purpose in this respect, it will be entitled to the gratitude of the most interesting class of people.-
For all these reasons, I shall support the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
If the contents of the speech from the throne are reassuring and give us good reason to hope for the future, we cannot, however, overlook die dark clouds which still threaten on the horizon. Too often do we hear birds of ill-'omen croaking every type of propaganda intended to fray our nerves and fill us with anxiety for the future of our country and the social security of our people.	.
I wish to denounce the proponents of extreme imperialism and of a policy of immigration on a vast scale. There are also the proponents of state controls whom I intend to denounce when opportunity offers. It is certain that, once the war is over, our people will balk at all the vexatious restrictions imposed by a new bureaucracy, which must be done away with as soon as possible.
The Canadian people believe that they are at home in Canada. They are ceaselessly reminded that they are a sovereign state and that the Westminster statute is a step in the road to independence. If so, be they allowed to keep their delusions and let there be a stop to the procession of salesmen of imperialism who come with statements hurtful to Canadian sentiments.
I congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for having disapproved of the terms of Lord Halifax's last proposal. Let the latter attend to his mission in the United States and abstain from offering us suggestions of an imperial federation. If the former leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) and the present leader (Mr. Graydon) have refused to take a positive stand on these matters, it is probably because his views expressed follow very closely those of the Tory party, as foriherly expressed by Lord Bennett, of whom we have such an unpleasant recollection. One may be convinced that this policy of imperialization is not accepted any more by the proud people of Canada.
While still shouting that nothing matters except the winning of the war, an attempt is made, in certain quarters, to take advantage
of the willingness of our country to go the limit on the road to sacrifice to ask that further sacrifices be made to promote the interests of foreign nations, when peace has been won. An incidious propaganda is spreading the idea that Canada, with its 3,500,000 square miles of territory, should accommodate all the refugees from other countries who wish to take their chances in our midst. In my humble view, this proposition is for the least premature. In spite of their traditionally charitable dispositions, our people will oppose the entry of outsiders, from whatever country they may come, until our returned men and our unemployed have secured jobs bringing them enough money to ensure their welfare and the stabilization of our commerce and industry. Personally, I would resent it if strangers were to take the places, on this hemisphere, that rightly belong to .Canadians.
A lot is said about devastation and ruin in countries that have fallen victims to aggression. Our help and sympathy have so far gone to those countries, but do you not believe, Mr. Speaker, that their reconstruction will call for the efforts of all their sons? Should Canada send her people abroad for reconstruction work, while refugees who should logically be at work in their own countries, would take the place of our people in Canada and enjoy here a more comfortable life? That would be absurd.
The complaint is heard that some European countries have a too low birth-rate. Would not their problem become more acute if they were deprived of the elements necessary for the restoration of their population? After the war, each country wall have to set its own house in order.
I have received many protest petitions from my constituency and I fully intend to support them. May I suggest that all those advocates of mass immigration should be strongly advised to stop their agitation and wait until our country's economic and industrial structure recovers from the injuries it has sustained before they put forward any immigration plan. We must show forbearance, but I still believe in the old motto, which the British have taught us by word and deed: Charity begins at home. To sacrifice the interests of our people to those of outsiders, would be ill directed charity while being detrimental, at the same time, to the countries of those who would benefit by our excessive generosity.
I have made these few remarks in the house in order to call the attention of the hon. members to the serious disturbance that might be engendered in our country by the implementation of a policy advocated by Utopians prompted by momentary enthusiasm, without a thought for the real interests of our people.

These thoughts have been inspired by one single hope, that of seeing Canada, after the war, once again a unified, happy and prosperous country.
